name: Tribulus terrestris
short: Case reports: severe liver and kidney injury, seizure, priapism needing surgery, muscle breakdown with atorvastatin. Trials in men with erectile dysfunction: adverse events like placebo.
text: Case reports describe serious harms in people taking tribulus: severe jaundice with kidney dysfunction and drug-induced liver injury on biopsy in a 46-year-old man after 2 months of daily supplements, treated with plasmapheresis, who recovered (the report notes the plant has been linked to severe jaundice and death in grazing animals); acute kidney injury requiring dialysis in a 43-year-old man with a history of self-administered herbal medicine use, who survived and recovered (the report is titled as being about tribulus, and its abstract names tribulus as an example of a widely used herbal medicine, but it does not say that this patient took it); severe hyperbilirubinaemia followed by acute renal failure in a young man after ingesting tribulus; liver, kidney and nerve toxicity with a seizure in a man who drank the herbal water for 2 days to prevent kidney stones, improving after he stopped; a 72-hour priapism after a tribulus supplement, treated surgically and followed by negative effects on sexual function (the abstract does not say for how long); and gynaecomastia in a young weight-trainer after a herbal tablet taken by mouth (tribulus is named only in the report's title). In contrast, in trials in men with erectile dysfunction, a meta-analysis of 8 randomized studies found no difference in adverse events between tribulus and placebo, and a 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in 180 men found no difference in adverse events and no drug-related serious adverse events; a systematic review of 7 studies in physically active men reported no tribulus-induced toxicity and no significant changes in kidney markers. For interactions, a case report describes rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) with mild liver enzyme rises in a 71-year-old man taking tribulus with long-term atorvastatin, and its authors say tribulus may be a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor affecting statin metabolism; a retrospective review of adverse-event reports linked tribulus with antidepressants to generalised itching (citalopram), galactorrhoea (escitalopram) and a psoriasis relapse (trazodone).
